en: The boy paid no heed to death.
Semetey grew angry,
Exerted his strength fiercely,
From Camel Wrestler's hand
The lord's son, the lone hero,
Drew out his forearm.
Now Camel Wrestler extended his forearm.
Then we saw, people,
The terror Semetey could bring.
With a slap, he seized
Camel Wrestler's forearm.
Trying to pull, he could not pull free;
Camel Wrestler fidgeted.
Trying to wrench away, he could not;
Camel Wrestler squirmed.
He tightened his grip again;
Camel Wrestler began to shuffle.
“Ah, mercy! Ah!” he cried.
“We submit to you as slaves!” he said,
Cowering before Semetey.
From the tips of his five fingers—
Did you see his might?—
Dark blood, enough for a mare's milking,
Spurted and streamed.
“And you called yourself a wrestler!”
The descendant of the blood-drinker
Seized him again,
Five times harder than before,
Gripped him with greater force.
Poor Camel Wrestler's
Teeth began to grind.
One of Camel Wrestler's arms,
Like a rotten reed,
Broke to pieces with a crack.
Camel Wrestler lost his strength.
The famed sacred capital of sheikhs,
Populous Kokand and Margilan,
Below them, Andijan,
The people of four khans gathered.
Before they could bring gifts,
Before they could somehow
Plead for the wrestler's blood,
Before they could intervene,
Your boy now found his chance.
Lifting him like a feedbag,
Poor Camel Wrestler
He dashed to the earth.
Not letting the wrestler stir,
He pressed down upon his belly.
The orphan began his terrible deed;
One of Camel Wrestler's arms
He tore clean out.
Then poor Camel Wrestler died.
Semetey's prowess
The eight khans observed.
What could the eight poor khans do?
They ran up and down.
“He truly takes after his father!” they said;
The eight khans despaired of their lives.
Then the orphan came to maturity;
Thus he joined the ranks.
He grew to manhood and became a hero;
Your boy became the equal of a hero's son.
Cursed be his becoming a hero!
Now his affairs have gone badly.
Let me not tell it, let you not hear it, brother-in-law!
Give thanks to God;
Now be content with God, brother-in-law!
Who bears it, who does not,
What the Creator lays upon one's head?
Let us recite the Quran
For your boy who has passed away, dear brother-in-law.
Between the dead and the living,
Brother-in-law, the Quran alone goes between.
At the great feast in Bukhara,
No one remained to turn a catching pole against your boy.
Alas, such is this shitty world!
He emerged a lion protected by Shai,
His twelve bodily members sound,
Of Manas who passed away,
He emerged a hero equal to the man himself.
The eight khans ate at his feast.
“If this child lives,
He will overturn the world,” they said.
When he threw Camel Wrestler,
When he tore out one of his arms,
Had someone's tongue struck the boy?
Had someone's evil eye struck him?
Your boy was stricken in the ribs,
Your only son felt it at the crown of his head.
A sickness no one could discover struck him;
He met with a true pestilence.
His cup-like liver was crushed,
Blood came from his mouth.
No resourceful healer could be found;
No remedy at all was found for your boy.
He has seen the face of eternity;
Your only son died seven days ago!
Then the God who strikes down
Struck him utterly, so I heard.
‘My little camel calf!’ sobbing,
Burning with grief, weeping and crying,
His own beard, Temir Khan,
Poor man, tore it out, so I heard.
‘I will not outlive my only one,’ she said;
His grandmother Chiyyrdy,
An old woman of ninety-five,
Fell upon a knife and wounded herself,
And died, so I heard.
His own father Ismail
Smashed his own head,
Struck himself, so I heard.
That grieving woman Kanykei,
‘My only one, whom I mourn, has died!’ she said,
Striking both her cheeks,
Tore at them, so I heard.
Her unmerciful, wretched life
She tormented, so I heard.
The eight khans who came to the feast,
All eight khans,
‘Now Manas is truly dead!’ they said,
And left weeping, so I heard.
Now be content with God;
Brother-in-law, give thanks to God.
“Brother-in-law, your Talas has been left deserted;
Thus your Manas has gone without an heir!”
Without speaking a word, without uttering a sound,
When he heard this news,
Khan Bakai lost his voice.
His two eyes staring wildly,
Khan Bakai lost his speech.
After the time it takes to cook meat, he began to speak,
Speaking softly but firmly:
“Valley upon valley, little valley, my child,
Settle in a little valley, my child.
Bereft of the one who loves you,
Become like me yourself, my child!
Your dark mouth filled with blood,
My child, come to a day beyond return!
May God cool your breath;
Become like that Semetey yourself!
My child, settle along a barren pass;
May God cool your breath,
Bereft of the one who loves you,
My child, become like me yourself!”
Khan Bakai uttered his curse,
Now spoke words of desolation.
Making the dark earth weep,
Bakai began to lament his only one:
“My spring that feeds a flowing river,
My lamp, gained through mortal hardship!
My only Semetey, my little one!
My plump, gray-mottled hawk,
My morning star left by my friend Manas!
My fortress with walls of iron,
My little camel calf who left me burning with grief,
Semetey, may I be your sacrifice, my scourge!
My beloved comfort left by Manas,
My mirror, may I be your sacrifice!
My hoof left by a courser,
For this beakless, wretched soul,
My little one whom I made my support.
My pennant fastened to a spear,
Semetey, my gift left by the magnanimous one,
Alas upon alas, my little camel calf!
Semetey, where shall I see you!
Valley upon valley, little valley,
Have I settled along the valley?
Bereft of my only one,
O God, have I become like an extinguished fire?
Did I think I would raid Samarkand?
Bereft of my only one,
Have I bitten my beard today!
I herd camels, I roam far;
My only one left by my lord,
Alas, I wonder whether he will come.
Making Kökcholok saddle-sore,
When I have grown old,
Hurting my heart,
Exhausting the light of my eyes,
For whose sake do I pray?
Watching and herding camels,
For you alone, Semetey!
I have heard ill news of you.
My only one, dark is your day—take me with you!
Have you turned your neck toward death?
This uncle of yours who cannot die,
Have you made him like an extinguished fire!
At Kökötöi's memorial feast,
Before the great assembly,
When Koshoi gave his blessing,
Unbelievers and Muslims,
When they gave their blessing together,
You were a child conceived through blessing,
Left behind by my King Manas.
Alas, orphan, take me with you!
In the whiteness of my beard,
Alas, while my journey still remains,
Why did my wretched life not end without distress?
Why have I not seen the face of eternity?
‘Fortunate Bakai has died,’ they might have said,
Had I died before you,
You did not come lamenting, orphan;
With your own hands, your uncle
You did not bury with due splendor.
Alas, orphan, take me with you!
I did not see you before I died!
I grieved while herding camels;
I have lost the one who loved me.
My morning star beside the moon,
My cherished kinsman and support,
My poor one, his father's only son,
To Temir Khan's city
My nightingale wandered and died.
My poor one who departed young,
My hawk, alone in the nest,
Hearing news of you, I was undone.
In my old age, I, Bakai,
Howled like a hungry wolf.
My true plane tree has been felled,
My wretched beard has thinned;
Have I consumed my good fortune now?
I herded camels and roamed far.
My only one left by my lord,
I wondered whether he would come.
I herded camels for his sake;
I wore myself out for the child left by my lord.
My goatskin coat upon my flesh,
My leather trousers upon my arse,
I went seeking Jelmayan.
The enemy cut off my beard;
I heard the news of my orphan!
I have been bereft through ill news.
Take me with you, orphan, take me!
Turning back from herding camels,
God has now struck me upon the head.
Bereft of my orphan,
I, Bakai, burn with this ill news.
Orphan who loved me, take me with you!
O luckless beard,
You have become as though shorn!
Poor staring eyes,
Have you become as though gouged out?
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol, broad Talas,
Have you become as though burned?
Blood-shedding Manas, would that you had not died!
Would that this head had not seen desolation!
My king dead, everyone dead,
Today Bakai too is dead.
While my king was still alive,
Why did I not die before him?!
When we raided Ombu and took spoils,
While my scourge was still alive,
Breaking through their midst and making a road,
My blue-gray lynx and marten-fur cap
Swaying upon me,
